item.title: More Than 40 Dead After a Ferry Capsizes on Zimbabwe’s Lake Kariba
item.description:
At least 44 people are dead and an unknown number are still missing a day after a crowded ferry overturned in Zimbabwe’s Lake Kariba, the country’s president said on Wednesday.

“It is with a heavy heart and profound sadness that I learned of the tragic capsizing,” said Emmerson Mnangagwa, president of Zimbabwe, in a statement on Wednesday about the accident, which occurred on Tuesday and has raised questions about the ferry’s safety and operations.

He thanked private citizens and government security teams, noting that “without their swift response, many more lives would have been lost in the rough and choppy conditions” on the lake that day.

While dozens of people have been rescued — at least 67, the Zimbabwe police said — the search for more missing continued through Wednesday and will resume on Thursday.

Still, just how many passengers may have been on board the ferry when it capsized is unclear, the authorities say. There are indications that the vessel was packed well beyond its designated capacity, the police noted.

The ferry was run by the Rural Infrastructure Development Agency, a quasi-governmental department tasked with the development and maintenance of infrastructure, water supplies, roads services and more. The boat had an official capacity of 90 passengers, excluding crew, but initial indications suggested there were about 120 passengers on the vessel when it overturned, according to the national police.

Based on their investigations, the police suspect the true number could have been even higher, officials said.

The vessel left from the resort town of Kariba and was headed to Chalala, a remote fishing camp on the shores of Lake Kariba, which is the world’s largest man-made lake by volume. According to a declaration of disaster by the president, it capsized after being struck by strong waves while navigating near Long Island, an island about 10 miles from Kariba.

The Department of Civil Protection is coordinating a search and rescue response with the national police’s underwater unit, the Zimbabwe National Army Boat Squadron, local authorities and others. A privately owned helicopter from the Matusadonha Conservation Trust, a national park, has also been deployed to support aerial search efforts, according to the presidential declaration.

Zimbabwe’s public broadcaster said on Wednesday evening that search and rescue operations had stopped for the night and would resume again on Thursday, with divers concerned that there were still people trapped inside the capsized ferry. It said that there are plans to tow the ferry to a nearby island.

“This tragedy has exposed serious deficiencies in our maritime capabilities which we have to address immediately so that our places of recreation do not become death traps to the innocent,” Mr. Mnangagwa said, in an apparent reference to the ferry being overcrowded. And he directed all agencies associated with maritime safety, including specialized units within the security forces, “to take an active interest in ensuring remedial interventions” in light of Tuesday’s accident.

Mr. Mnangagwa called on Zimbabweans to “unite in prayer for the souls of the departed, for the success of the ongoing search operations, speedy recovery of survivors and for comfort and strength for the bereaved families.”

item.title: Arabian Sea Bird and Turtle Habitat Threatened by Oil From Grounded Tanker
item.description:
An oil spill from a Russian shadow fleet tanker that ran aground two months ago has spread its long, black tongue across a remote, ecologically sensitive swath of the Arabian Sea, according to satellite data and statements from Oman’s government.

The spill has encircled the rocky cliffs of an Omani island, Jazirat al Qibliyah, that is home to a range of endangered seabirds, and spread to a 25-mile stretch of beach on the mainland, called Ras Madrakah, Oman’s environmental agency said Wednesday in a statement carried by the state news agency.

A British maritime disaster management company, called Ambrey, has been hired to rescue the tanker and stop the spread of the spill, according to the company. “This is an extremely challenging situation, compounded by adverse weather conditions,” said Ed Wollaston, director of global response at Ambrey.

The spill compounds the environmental consequences of three widening, overlapping conflicts that have made oil and gas infrastructure targets of war in recent months. Russia and Ukraine have attacked each other’s energy facilities. In Yemen, the Houthi militia has attacked oil tankers tied to Saudi Arabia. And the United States and Iran have attacked oil installations and tankers in and around the Strait of Hormuz.

Several oil spills have been detected from satellite images in the strait, including a fairly significant one off Iran’s Kharg island, according to Brian Barnes, a geographer at the University of South Florida. None of them are anywhere near as large as the massive spills of the 1991 Gulf war, when Iraqi forces set ablaze hundreds of oil wells and caused one of the world’s worst environmental catastrophes, which took years to clean up. But swift cleanups are impossible with the ongoing conflict, and even the ecological impacts of the spills are hard to gauge at the moment.

“Satellite observations are great and can tell us a lot,” Mr. Barnes said. “But we don’t have the capacity to go out and see.”

On Tuesday, Iranian state media posted images of oil contamination spreading to Qeshm Island, including an area, known as Shib Deraz, where the rare hawksbill sea turtle nests every spring. Iranian government officials have said nothing about the cause of that spill.

The spill in Omani waters appears to be among the largest of several in the waterways of the Middle East. Estimates vary widely on the scale of the contamination, and what caused it in the first place remains a mystery. All that is certain is that Oman’s government has been forced to respond, because the tanker crashed into the rocky shoals of Qibliyah on a windy day in June.

It seems to have had little to do with Oman, or the conflicts in the region.

The tanker, known as the Caroline Bezengi, is about 900 feet long and capable of carrying nearly a million barrels of oil. It had been used for the last couple of years to ferry Russian crude oil to refineries in Asia, according to TankerTrackers.com, a company that monitors global oil shipping.

In the past, it was flagged under Cameroon. Its managing agent was a firm registered in Cyprus, called Lagosmarine, which was under sanctions by the United States and European Union for helping finance Russia’s war in Ukraine.

Since May, 2023, it had made 12 trips from ports in Russia to ports in India and Pakistan, and once to China, according to logs kept by TankerTrackers.com. In 2025, its crew had complained of not being paid for months, the Seafarers Union of Russia told Russian media outlets.

Its latest journey began on May 13 from the Russian port of Novorossiysk, on the Black Sea, according to TankerTrackers.com. It was headed for Sikka, a port on the western coast of India that serves the world’s largest refinery complex, near Jamnagar.

India, which has not signed on to Western sanctions imposed after Russia’s invasion of Ukraine, has instead sharply increased its purchase of Russian oil since that war began in 2022.

India’s growing economy needs a lot of oil, and its refineries, including the Jamnagar complex, have made a thriving business from exporting refined products to fuel-hungry countries.

The Caroline Bezengi did not reach India this time.

On June 6, the ship encountered “an incident” outside Oman’s territorial waters, the head of the country’s Environment Authority, Abdullah Bin Ali Al Amri, said in an interview on Oman TV.

Whether the incident was caused by malfunctioning equipment on the ship or by an attack remains unknown. No party has accepted responsibility.

By June 21, according to the Omani government, the ship ran aground on the rocks of the Qibliyah Island. “Reconnaissance measures were taken to inspect the ship’s safety, and indeed, at that time, there was no noticeable oil spill,” Mr. Al Amri said in the television interview.

By late July, there was a noticeable spill. By early August, it had spread.

Oman’s Environment Authority said this week that the slick covers around 390 square kilometers.

Greenpeace said that by Aug. 4 it had covered 600 square kilometers, a fourfold increase in just two days. “The situation surrounding the tanker Caroline Bezengi is yet another alarming example of the serious environmental risks posed by Russia’s so-called shadow fleet,” the organization said in a statement.

John Amos, head of an organization called SkyTruth, which uses satellite imagery to track oil contamination, estimated the coverage area to have grown to roughly 2,200 square kilometers. He said the Omani government’s estimate appears “far too low.”

Mr. Amos said if all of the Caroline Bezengi’s oil leaked, the spill would be comparable to the Exxon Valdez disaster, one of the worst spills in American history that killed hundreds of thousands of seabirds, otters, seals and whales.

Ambrey, the maritime response firm, said in a statement to The New York Times that it was working with the Omani Air Force to stabilize the ship and that ships to help with the salvage operation were en route.

Shadow fleet tankers are often uninsured, and shipowners rarely come forward. Oman is left with the task of monitoring and stanching the damage. The Environment Authority, in its latest statement on Monday, said the slick was advancing quickly in a northeasterly direction.

It said it was trying to protect the most environmentally sensitive areas. “Efforts are being directed towards identifying zones most vulnerable to impact and correlating them with pollution drift trajectories, with particular emphasis on areas of high ecological value and sensitivity,” the ministry said.

Zane Irwin and Ismaeel Naar contributed reporting

item.title: What to Know About Today’s U.K. Special Election: Farage vs. Binface
item.description:
Nigel Farage, the leader of Reform U.K., Britain’s populist right-wing party, will face voters on Thursday in a special election that he initiated, hoping to return to Parliament weeks after resigning amid investigations into possible financial impropriety.

Mr. Farage, who is under investigation for failing to declare a 5 million pound gift (about $6.7 million) from a British crypto-billionaire in Thailand, has said he hopes that a new mandate from his constituents in Clacton, a coastal area in Essex, England, will show that his voters do not care about the issue.

He said that he has been the subject of “constant demonization” by the press and his critics. The investigations into his finances, he claims, are proof that the “establishment have now decided that they can’t beat us fairly, so they’ve chosen to use foul means.”

After he resigned to force the new special election, all of Britain’s major parties boycotted it, calling it a stunt. Mr. Farage’s most significant opponent is a novelty candidate named Count Binface, who campaigns wearing a trash can over his head.

Here’s what to know about Thursday’s vote.

As the leader of Reform U.K., Mr. Farage is the most prominent right-wing populist in Britain, focused on campaigning against immigration and in favor of lower taxes and fewer regulations, particularly on cryptocurrency.

A veteran politician who campaigned for more than two decades for Britain to leave the European Union, and who has led several parties, Mr. Farage is an ally of President Trump and has styled himself in a similar way. He has long warned of an “invasion” of migrants and railed against the establishment in Westminster.

For most of the last year, Reform led national opinion polls amid widespread concern about rising prices, taxes, migration and dissatisfaction with Keir Starmer, the former Labour prime minister.

In May, Mr. Farage led Reform to its biggest electoral success ever. The party won almost 1,500 seats on municipal councils. But overall, Reform won only about 26 percent of the vote, down from more than 30 percent the previous year.

And the party has lost several parliamentary by-elections that it had hoped to win in recent months, including in Gorton and Denton, which was won by the Green Party, and in Makerfield, where Labour’s Andy Burnham easily beat the Reform candidate.

The polls have shown a continued decline for Reform in recent weeks, as the accusations about improper disclosure of financial support have increased. Several recent polls have shown support for the party falling under 25 percent and Labour taking the lead.

Earlier this year, Britain’s parliamentary standards commissioner, Daniel Greenberg, confirmed that he was investigating whether Mr. Farage had broken parliamentary rules by not disclosing the £5 million gift from Christopher Harborne, the crypto billionaire.

Mr. Farage has said he did not need to disclose the gift, but has offered a variety of conflicting explanations for why Mr. Harborne gave him the money in the weeks before he won his seat in Parliament in 2024.

He initially said it was for his personal security amid threats. In his resignation speech, he said that he gets “daily online calls for me to be murdered” and has run up “very, very substantial bills to make sure that I was safe.”

But in an interview in May, Mr. Farage said the money was “a reward for campaigning for Brexit.”

Critics of Mr. Farage have pointed out that since he entered Parliament, he has championed the cryptocurrency industry and that Reform has pushed for light-touch regulation.

In his resignation speech, Mr. Farage referred to the standards investigation into the Harborne gift, but also said that “yet another standards investigation is underway.” That comment came days after The Sunday Times of London reported that one of his close aides, George Cottrell, had provided undisclosed benefits to Mr. Farage including security, social media employees and accommodation.

Mr. Farage did not intend to stay out of office for long.

In his remarks last month announcing his resignation, he said that “the people of Clacton should be the judges of my actions. This will be a people-versus-the-establishment by-election. It’s a chance to stick two fingers up to the entire establishment, to frankly tell them where to go.”

Reform officials were always very confident that Mr. Farage would recapture his seat in Parliament. The last time he ran in Clacton, during the 2024 general election, he won with 46.2 percent of the vote. The Conservative Party candidate came second with 27.9 percent.

But Mr. Farage and his advisers hoped to use the election to change the political narrative and give him a prominent victory over his major rival political parties. Instead, all of the main parties said they would not put forward candidates, preferring to wait for the results of the parliamentary investigation.

That makes it more likely that Mr. Farage will win a landslide, while making it harder for him to argue that he defeated “the establishment.”

Count Binface is a character played by Jon Harvey, 46, a writer and comedian who is part of Britain’s long tradition of novelty political candidates. He describes himself as an intergalactic space warrior from the planet Sigma IX. His campaign pledges include a promise to build “at least one affordable house” and to “cut your taxes and raise everyone else’s.”

Mr. Harvey — or, as he’s better known, Mr. Binface — has run in several recent elections. In the recent special election where Prime Minister Andy Burnham won with 24,927 votes, Mr. Binface received just 95. (Though that was more than twice the number of votes that Howling Laud Hope received as the candidate for the Official Monster Raving Loony Party.)

In a recent interview in The New York Times, Mr. Binface said, “If humans choose to vote for Nigel, that is democracy.” But with the major parties absent, “I seem to be his majesty’s opposition.”

He is not expected to win on Thursday.

Assuming that Mr. Farage wins, as expected, he will once again be a member of Parliament. But the investigations into his finances — and those of Reform U.K. — are unlikely to be resolved any time soon.

The parliamentary standards investigation could continue for weeks or months.

If the standards investigation concludes that Mr. Farage violated Parliament’s rules, he could be suspended, possibly prompting another special election. The Conservative Party has already said it would run a candidate in Clacton if that happens.

There is also a police investigation underway into the legality of two donations to Reform of £250,000 each from Mr. Cottrell’s mother, Fiona. In a statement last month, the Metropolitan Police said that two people had been questioned as part of the investigation, although no arrests have been made. Reform did not respond to requests for comment. Mr. Cottrell and Ms. Cottrell could not be reached for comment.

item.title: Early-Onset El Niño
item.description:
About 1,000 miles south of Hawaii, the first signs of El Niño have come to Kiribati, an island nation in the central Pacific Ocean.

Alyssa Atwood, an associate professor in the Earth, ocean and atmospheric science department at Florida State University, is there now, deploying sensors to monitor ocean heat and salinity, and to track the bleaching of the area’s magnificent coral reefs.

Already, around Christmas Island, one of this nation’s 33 atolls and islands, the ocean surface temperature is 2 degrees Celsius, or 3.6 degrees Fahrenheit, warmer than usual for this time of year, compared with the previous 30 years. And as much as 10 percent of the corals appeared bleached in a series of dives over the past few days, Atwood said.

Bleaching occurs when corals become so stressed that they lose the symbiotic algae they need to survive. Bleached corals can recover, but if the surrounding water stays too hot for too long, they die.

“We expect this to get worse and worse and worse until the end of this year,” she said. “This is just the tip of the iceberg.”

That’s because the El Niño event that’s underway is expected to be one of the strongest ever recorded, and it has not yet peaked.

El Niño is a naturally occurring surge of heat in the Pacific Ocean that usually reaches maximum intensity between December and February. It happens every two to seven years, and it typically spikes global temperatures and scrambles weather patterns around the world.

This year’s event is already strong and having big effects, nudging up global temperatures and causing dry spells and crop failures on multiple continents, my colleagues Raymond Zhong and Chico Harlan wrote in an article this week.

While scientists expect this to be a very strong El Niño, it’s still not entirely clear whether man-made global warming is intensifying the phenomenon.

The El Niños of the past few decades have been comparably strong, Ray and Chico wrote. But the variables that combine to create an El Niño are complex, and some experts argue that the recent trend could just be a random signal.

What is clear is that El Niño’s burst of heat, boosted by climate change or not, is arriving at a moment when global temperatures are already at record highs.

As Eric Niiler wrote in a separate article this year, the past 11 years have been the hottest since record-keeping began. Last year was either the second or third hottest on record, depending on which record is used, he reported, with global average temperatures 1.43 degrees Celsius higher than preindustrial levels. The year 2024 was the hottest, at 1.55 degrees Celsius above the preindustrial average.

All that heat has led to more intense storms, floods, fires and droughts. All of which could become even more intense in the months ahead.

El Niño will magnify those conditions in some regions and could lift global temperatures to record levels next year, as the heat from the Pacific spreads around the world, Ray and Chico wrote.

Atwood said she hoped the data she was gathering in Kiribati could help scientists understand how man-made global warming is affecting El Niños.

“We don’t know what the human fingerprint is on these systems, which is why we have to be out here actually measuring these things in real time, documenting them as much as possible,” she said. “Because these things are happening now on top of background warming in the climate system.”

In Kiribati, El Niño appears to be taking a toll already. Christmas Island, usually very dry this time of year, has been battered by heavy rainfall in recent weeks. During the last very strong El Niño, from 2015 to 2016, heavy rains in the country led to an uptick in mosquito-borne illnesses, including dengue fever and chikungunya virus.

And back then, more than 90 percent of the coral reef around Christmas Island was bleached. The good news, Atwood said, is that much of that coral has recovered over the past decade.

In Panama, normally one of the wettest countries on Earth, some areas haven’t had a major storm since early May. Ethiopia’s fertile highlands are enduring one of their driest summer stretches in four decades. And India had its fifth-driest June since the country’s modern rain records began in 1901.

“It affects weather all around the globe,” Atwood said. “And the bigger the event, the more pronounced those effects get.”

In the coming months, we’ll bring you regular updates about how this event is reshaping the globe and what the science tells us about the climate connection. So stay tuned.

The Trump administration has pulled federal funding for an annual report on the changing environment of the Arctic, where rapid warming is upending ecosystems, reconfiguring trade routes and scrambling geopolitics.

The assessment, known as the Arctic Report Card, drew on the expertise of hundreds of scientists and other specialists around the world. Every year for the past two decades, it provided a checkup on the health of the region, which is heating up at several times the pace of the rest of the globe. Sea ice has dwindled. Snow cover has shrunk. Glaciers are thinning out. Tundra vegetation has grown more abundant, leading to wildfires that burn through huge areas. — Raymond Zhong

Read more.

Delegates from around the world are gathering in Mongolia for United Nations talks on stopping desertification, Climate Home News reports.

Marathon organizers are adjusting to warmer race conditions by shifting dates, starting earlier and offering runners shorter alternatives, according to The Associated Press.

item.title: Electric Thrills
item.description:
It’s Friday, and as promised I have something fun for you: My colleague Chico Harlan, our global climate correspondent, is taking you on a high-adrenaline motorcycle ride through Lahore. And not just on any motorcycle. The bike he rode was electric — as are an increasing number of motorcycles on the streets of Pakistan.

Thrills aside, Chico’s reporting shows something intriguing: The war in Iran has sped up the clean energy transition. In the countries most vulnerable to higher gasoline prices, like Pakistan, the most common vehicles tend to have two wheels, not four. In those countries, the electric motorcycle era has arrived. Hang on tight!

By Chico Harlan

I went to Pakistan last month to learn about the country’s electric motorcycle boom.

Electric motorcycles scarcely existed in Pakistan three years ago, but now sales are surging. The switch signals how quickly, and perhaps permanently, people in developing countries are pivoting away from fossil fuels as the war in Iran keeps oil prices high.

I visited showrooms and an assembly plant and interviewed company founders and would-be buyers. As the trip neared its end, I figured I’d learned just about everything I needed to know.

Except what it feels like to actually ride one.

“Do you want take it out for a drive?” Abdul Rafay, the owner of a new Vlektra electric motorcycle, asked me after we finished an interview.

I looked out at the city of 14 million, as motorbikes pinballed around rickshaws and four-wheelers, and muttered something about journalists not making themselves a part of the story.

But OK, I’d accept a ride. I borrowed a helmet and climbed on the back of Rafay’s bike, just one among the hundreds of thousands of newish, gasoline-free vehicles humming along across Pakistan.

E-bikes and war

Electric motorcycles, it turns out, are a good indicator of the changes driven by the war in Iran. That’s because in poorer countries, where people are most vulnerable to energy-price shocks, two-wheelers are far more common than cars.

Electric vehicles typically cost more to buy than gasoline-powered versions. But rising gasoline prices have given electrics a big advantage: It’s much cheaper to charge a battery than to fill up a fuel tank.

In Vietnam, where the streets teem with motorcycles, the biggest domestic producer, VinFast, has reported soaring sales. In Kenya, about 25 to 35 percent of new motorcycle sales are electric, said Gagan Gupta, the founder of Spiro, the largest electric vehicle company operating in Africa. He said the war’s energy shock had helped “multiply everything by two times.”

People in the industry increasingly talk up the idea that future generations will never operate gasoline-powered vehicles. “The demand is effectively open-ended,” said Josh Whale, the founder of Ampersand, an electric motorcycle company that operates in Kenya and Rwanda.

In Pakistan, motorbikes make up about 80 percent of vehicles on the road and are often the most valuable thing a person owns. The new proliferation of electric motorcycles comes from a mix of homegrown ingenuity and China’s manufacturing prowess.

Some Pakistani companies use chassis and tires manufactured domestically, and batteries and motors from China. But other companies depend on China almost entirely. They import ready-to-assemble bikes that need little more than a logo. Pakistan, aiming to clear up its polluted skies, imposes duties of only 1 percent on such imports.

Sales of electric two-wheelers rose 173 percent during the first half of the year in Pakistan, according to a market data firm, thanks to a government subsidy program and the increase in oil prices that came with the U.S. war with Iran.

“Trump is the biggest salesman — salesman of the year,” said Muhammad Salman, managing director of Yadea Pakistan, the national distributor of Yadea bikes, one of the major brands in China.

‘You got scared, didn’t you?’

On the bike, I hung on tight as Rafay, 24, merged into a roundabout. We were in a relatively upscale part of the city, with painted lane markers and smooth roads. But drivers in Pakistan, I think it can be said, have a strong stomach for adventure.

Rafay clearly wanted to show off his new bike’s power. So he seized on a small opening and accelerated past a rickshaw. He zipped toward two orange vehicles, two or three feet apart. As Rafay darted toward them, a gap opened just large enough to let us through.

The video I was taking with my iPhone doesn’t convey my visceral certainty that one of those orange vehicles was going to clip my knee.

I’d clenched my legs hard enough that Rafay could feel it.

“You got scared, didn’t you?” he asked, looking back.

“Yes,” I said, heart racing a bit, but happy.

Rafay, a gearhead, said he’d loved his previous motorcycle, a Honda CD 70, Pakistan’s most popular gas model. He’d driven it more than 60 kilometers each day to and from his job as a software engineer. But then gasoline costs soared and he started thinking about the math.

“If I can save a few rupees,” he said, “I’ll do it.”

After my ride with Rafay, I thanked him for driving so capably and handed back the helmet.

Then, before the next rains came, I returned to the gas-powered Toyota car I’d been using for the week. It was a vehicle that never made me clench my knees.

Read the full story.

Europe sweltered in the fifth intense heat wave since May, with some temperatures soaring above 40 degrees Celsius. Some people in England are wondering what happened to their cool summers.

Vladimir Putin angered Japan with his first visit to islands the Soviet Union seized at the end of World War II.

Russian strikes on Ukrainian grain ships are once again threatening global food supplies.

An Australian jury found a former Catholic bishop guilty of sexually abusing two young Indigenous men in 2008.

The Israeli military evicted about a dozen settlers who had besieged two Palestinian families in their West Bank homes. Hours later, some of the settlers returned.

Social media tributes to Zhu Rongji, the former Chinese premier, yearned for a more hopeful era when the country was opening to the world.

My colleague Apoorva Mandavilli visited a factory in Brazil where scientists are producing mosquitoes that fight tropical diseases like dengue. Watch the video.

The most clicked link in your newsletter yesterday was about gadgets that keep you cool.

Although curling is decidedly a winter sport, a synthetic rink was set up in Rome in June. The surface is high-density plastic instead of ice. The stones weigh about a tenth of the regulation weight, and players use brooms to retrieve the stones rather than control their path. The goal? Get Romans to come out and play, despite the blistering heat.

Thousands of software developers across Africa have turned to Chinese A.I. models in the past year. My colleagues interviewed some of them to find out why.

Many developers said they wanted something that worked well on limited resources. They preferred Chinese systems, which anyone can download and modify without payment or approval. “Why use an expensive Ferrari to do the school run when a Toyota hatchback can do the same?” one Nairobi entrepreneur said. Read more about China’s A.I. surge in Africa.

In Bali, fireflies are revered as sacred messengers, a connection between living communities and their ancestors. But they’re disappearing across the Indonesian island because of climate change and environmental threats.

I Wayan Wardika has embarked on a quest to restore what he calls “the magic of fireflies.” He has started Indonesia’s first firefly conservation facility, where he breeds and raises them in terrariums named “honeymoon suites.” Read more and see the lab.

This version of the classic Southern lane cake takes all of fruitcake’s best elements — bourbon-soaked dried fruit, toasty pecans and shredded coconut — and weaves them into a rich, custardy filling set between three layers of tender vanilla cake. It’s a dessert and a nightcap, rolled into one.

Which island is this?

Naoshima, Japan

Sicily, Italy

Spitsbergen, Norway

Don Det, Laos

One of the things I love most about summer is that life slows down a little and I get to carve out time to read the books and listen to the podcasts that have piled up, literally and figuratively.

I’ll share some of my highlights in case you still have a bit of vacation time left.

My favorite nonfiction book this summer was “Peak Human” by Johan Norberg, a Swedish historian who tells the story of seven golden ages of humanity — including ancient Athens, the Abbasid Caliphate, the Song dynasty and the modern West. He explores what allowed humans to flourish in each of those periods and what we can learn from them today. (Spoiler alert: All of them were open to ideas and trade.)

My favorite novel was “The Safekeep” by Yael van der Wouden. I had to get used to the writing, which is sparse and self-conscious, and initially a little annoying, partly to channel the main character — a complicated, intensely controlling and, yes, annoying, woman. But two plot twists later, the book is kind of a masterpiece. The backdrop is post-Holocaust Europe. I won’t say more.

My favorite podcast was “The Gaza Chef,” a five-part documentary by Yassin Musharbash, an investigative journalist at the German weekly Die Zeit. It’s a compelling and balanced investigation into the death of Mahmud Almadhoun, who ran a soup kitchen in the northern Gaza Strip and was killed by an Israeli drone two years ago. I couldn’t say it better than the tagline of the podcast: “The question of why he had to die leads deep into the worrisome future of warfare.”

Musharbash once worked as a fixer for John le Carré and has written a series of novels himself. He knows how to tell a good story!

And finally, my favorite feel-good holiday song this year: “Love Chain” by Candi Staton, a summer classic. Enjoy!

Have a great weekend! — Katrin

item.title: Engine Blade Hit Jet Window Before Man Was Partly Sucked Outside, Report Says
item.description:
The flight in Greece last month climbed to about 16,000 feet, less than 10 minutes after takeoff, when the aircraft’s engine began vibrating.

The shaking intensified. A loud bang was heard and the cabin’s altitude warning alarm blared, and oxygen masks dropped for 149 passengers. One window shattered, and a 61-year-old man had his head sucked out the window, with his wife and other passengers pulling at his legs and body.

In a report released on Thursday, federal investigators said they had found a bird’s remains on a damaged engine fan from the flight, which was operated by Malta Air, a subsidiary of Ryanair. The engine’s blades had ricocheted across the fuselage and cracked the window, according to a preliminary investigation released by the National Transportation Safety Board, which conducted the investigation at the direction of Greek authorities.

The man, from Serbia, lived. He was hospitalized in Thessaloniki, Greece, with friction burns. His current condition is unclear.

The report offers insight into the terrifying moments aboard the flight to Memmingen, Germany, on a Boeing 737. The flight eventually returned to Thessaloniki International Airport.

The full investigation will take about a year to two years to complete, according to the N.T.S.B.

A representative with Ryanair declined to comment until the investigation is completed. A Boeing representative said it would continue to support the inquiry conducted by the N.T.S.B.

The flight attendants prepared for cabin service on July 10 when they heard and felt a “loud continuous vibration,” investigators said. They also reported a “small” amount of fog and smoke.

The passengers grabbed their oxygen masks when the crew noticed people standing and asking for help. The man was partly pulled outside before others pulled him to safety.

One passenger retrieved a metal box to cover the broken window. A doctor, another passenger aboard, treated the 61-year-old man, investigators said.

The engine’s fan blades had broken and struck the plane’s fuselage and another portion of the plane. The blade shattered the passenger’s window in Row 11 and damaged the plane’s exterior, investigators said.

The captain, who was not identified, had tallied 8,270 flight hours. A majority of flight time was spent with an aircraft the same make and model as the Ryanair plane at the center of the aviation inquiry, according to the report, and aviation tracking sites said the aircraft had been flying since 2008.

The engine’s fan blades had been inspected most recently in May, and employees did not flag any findings, according to the report.

The plane’s engine is suspected to have been hit by birds four times in the 12 months leading up to the strike last month, investigators said.

Bird strikes on planes are a common problem. Last year, six people aboard a tourist helicopter died after it was most likely struck by a flock of geese before crashing into the Hudson River near Jersey City, N.J.

item.title: After 2 Plasma Donor Deaths, Company Pauses Clinics in Canada
item.description:
A health care company that pays people for their blood plasma is pausing operations in Canada months after two donors died in Winnipeg, Manitoba.

The deaths, last October and in January, brought the scrutiny of Canada’s health regulator, politicians and the public toward Grifols, a Spanish company that operates Canada’s only for-profit plasma collection business at 17 clinics.

On Thursday, the company described that scrutiny as unwarranted and a reason for its move to stop collecting plasma in Canada temporarily.

“In light of the unfounded attention that has been focused on compensated plasma collection, Grifols has proactively and voluntarily decided to pause plasma collection activities,” the company said in an emailed statement. The pause goes into effect on Friday.

The company informed Health Canada, a federal department, of its decision on Wednesday, the same day that the regulator issued Grifols a notice that it had failed to meet compliance standards at a Winnipeg clinic.

“Canadians’ safety must always come first, and we welcome Grifols’s decision,” Emilie Gauduchon-Campbell, a spokeswoman for the health minister, said in a statement, adding that regulators found “several compliance concerns.”

Grifols has been operating its for-profit clinics in Canada since 2022, when it entered into an agreement with the Canadian Blood Services, the nonprofit group that manages the country’s blood supply, to increase the sourcing of plasma.

Some people rely on the extra money they make from donating plasma, which can be around 100 Canadian dollars per week, about $72. Grifols advertises that donors can earn up to 6,000 Canadian dollars, or about $4,400, each year. Plasma donation is considered safe and deaths are rare.

People can donate plasma more frequently than blood because after a donor’s blood is drawn, the plasma, a light yellow liquid, is separated from red blood cells, which are then transfused back into the donor. Rich in antibodies, plasma is an important ingredient in treatments for many rare conditions and chronic illnesses, and it is seeing a booming demand.

Grifols, which operates about 400 plasma collection clinics around the world, said it would resume operations in Canada after arriving at a “framework” with Health Canada and the Canadian Blood Services to support a “sustainable and robust plasma collection network” there, the company said in a statement.

Of the two people who died, only one, Rodiyat Alabede, a 22-year-old international student, has been identified by friends and family members. Ms. Alabede, who was studying to become a social worker, became unresponsive during her plasma donation in October and died soon after, according to Manitoba’s coroner.

In March, Grifols said it did not believe there was a link between Ms. Alabede’s death and the plasma withdrawal procedure.

Private operators looking to collect plasma in exchange for cash incentives were previously strongly opposed by the Canadian Blood Services, which was concerned that the plasma would be sold abroad, rather than being used to benefit patients in Canada.

Europe relies heavily on imported plasma products, in part because of regulations adopted by the European Union that say blood product donations should be unpaid.

item.title: Putin Visits Islands Seized from Japan in World War II, Angering Tokyo
item.description:
President Vladimir V. Putin of Russia on Thursday visited islands seized from Japan at the end of World War II for the first time, prompting an angry rebuke from Tokyo.

Mr. Putin used the visit to reassert Russia’s territorial claims and to protest Japan’s ongoing sanctions against Russia over the invasion of Ukraine. A day before the visit, he said that Russia’s claim to the islands was a “reality” that had been “enshrined in international documents.”

“We are not threatening Japan. We have absolutely no claims against it,” Mr. Putin said. “On the contrary, Japan has territorial claims against our country.”

The visit, which came as Russia held large-scale military exercises in the neighboring seas, was the latest flare-up in tensions between the two countries. Russia has been putting pressure on Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi, a defense hawk and critic of Moscow who was elected last year. She has pushed forward with Japan’s largest postwar defense buildup and sought closer ties with the United States.

Ms. Takaichi criticized the visit on Thursday, saying Japan had repeatedly warned Russian leaders to stay away from the islands, which are known in Russia as the southern Kuril Islands and in Japan as the Northern Territories. She described them as “an inherent part of Japan’s territory, both historically and under international law.”

She told reporters that Mr. Putin’s visit “hurts the feelings of the Japanese people and is absolutely unacceptable.” Japan’s foreign ministry said on Thursday that it had summoned Russia’s ambassador to protest the visit.

Japan traces its claims to the 17th century, but the Russians generally date their sovereignty to the waning days of World War II, when Soviet troops occupied the islands after Japan’s surrender in 1945. Japan and Russia never signed a formal peace treaty after the war.

The islands stretch from the southern tip of the Kamchatka Peninsula in eastern Russia to Hokkaido in the northernmost part of Japan. Mr. Putin visited an island that is called Iturup in Russian and Etorofu in Japanese. He toured a fish-processing complex and ate caviar. He also visited a hospital and a school, the Kremlin said in a statement, releasing photos of the Russian leader’s stops.

The governor of the Sakhalin region, which includes the islands, Valery Limarenko, accompanied Mr. Putin on the visit. Under a bright sun, Mr. Putin met residents of the region and hugged two young children, in footage posted online by a state news reporter who follows the Russian leader.

“Look at this great weather, it’s like a resort!” Mr. Putin said. One woman responded that such weather is very rare, noting that it is usually windy and foggy. “The weather is smiling on you,” she said.

Mr. Putin’s visit is part of a broader tour across Siberia and the Far East that he has been making ahead of the Russian parliamentary election next month.

On Wednesday, during a visit to Russia’s Pacific Fleet in Yuzhno-Sakhalinsk, Mr. Putin boarded the Varyag guided missile cruiser. He said Japan had placed “unprovoked sanctions” on his country over the conflict in Ukraine and singled out Russia as an enemy threat.

The trip marks Mr. Putin’s first visit to the region claimed by Japan in his quarter century rule. President Dmitry A. Medvedev visited one of the islands in 2010, becoming the first Russian or Soviet leader to do so. Japan denounced the visit and summoned the Russian ambassador to Japan in protest.

Previous Japanese leaders, including former Prime Minister Shinzo Abe, a mentor to Ms. Takaichi, made efforts to win back some of the territory.

But in 2019, hopes of a deal were dashed by Mr. Putin. He said that any agreement must have support from the public, which in Russia is strongly opposed to returning any islands to Japan.

Japan has made small efforts to improve relations with Russia in recent months, including sending a delegation of government officials to Moscow for trade talks and organizing cultural exchange trips. But it has maintained economic and trade sanctions against Moscow over the Ukraine war.

A recent investigation by The New York Times found that Russian military intelligence has been using Japan as a hub to source components for its war effort, exploiting weak Japanese espionage laws and high-tech industry.

Michito Tsuruoka, a professor at Keio University in Tokyo, said that Mr. Putin’s visit suggested that “there is no intention — particularly on the Russian side — to improve relations with Japan.”

“Russia’s narrative is that the deterioration of Japan-Russia relations is Japan’s fault,” he said. “From Japan’s perspective, of course, that is outrageous and untrue; the blame lies with Russia. It is essentially a case of ‘he said, she said,’ and Japan has no choice but to stand firm.”

Kiuko Notoya contributed reporting from Tokyo.

item.title: Two Seriously Injured When Train Derails in Southern England
item.description:
Two people were seriously injured Thursday afternoon when a passenger train derailed in East Sussex, England, the British Transport Police said in a statement.

Nine other people suffered less serious injuries in the incident, in which three of the train’s eight carriages left the tracks and flipped onto their sides. Officials said people who were trapped in those cars had since been evacuated.

Some of the injured were treated at the scene, while others were taken to local hospitals, officials said.

Pictures of train cars lying on their side, with emergency workers and others standing on the top of the carriages were being shared online.

“We’ve declared a major incident, and a significant emergency service response is ongoing at the scene,” said Ian Drummond-Smith, the assistant chief constable at the department. “But all passengers on the train have now been safely evacuated from the service.”

It was unclear what caused the accident, though pictures from the scene showed bent and twisted rails where the three train cars apparently skidded off the track.

Heidi Alexander, the British transport secretary, said in a statement on social media that she was “deeply concerned of reports of a derailment.”

Aerial video footage from a BBC helicopter showed three of the eight train cars lying on their side, with a fourth partly derailed. The other four cars appeared to be still upright on the tracks.

Rob Bradley, a passenger, told the BBC that the journey with his daughter had seemed normal until they felt the train speeding up abruptly.

The train “then started to rock, and at that point I knew something was very strange, and then our carriage actually jumped vertically upward and we could tell it was a derailment,” Mr. Bradley said. “The emergency brakes then went on, the train and everything got thrown forward.”

Mr. Bradley said he and his daughter were in one of the carriages that did not tip over. But he said he saw some people with blood on their clothes as he evacuated the train.

Southern Railway, the company that operates the train, confirmed the incident in a statement: “A train has derailed in the area between Haywards Heath and Lewes. Emergency services are making their way to the scene, and we are working out the impact this will have on our network.”

The company added, “If you are traveling between London and the East Coast, we advise against traveling.”

The derailment took place on a section of a rail line between London and southeastern England. Thursday was the hottest day of the year so far in Britain, with temperatures in one part of London reaching 38 degrees Celsius, or around 100 Fahrenheit.

The Rail Accident Investigation Branch, an independent government agency, said it would begin an investigation.

In a statement on social media, the agency said that it was “deploying a team of inspectors to the site of a passenger train derailment near to Lewes, East Sussex, to begin gathering evidence.”

Mr. Drummond-Smith, of the British Transport Police, said his department was “supporting the Rail Accident Investigation Branch to establish exactly what’s happened. We’ll provide further information as soon as we are able.”

item.title: Whatever Happened to English Summers? Scorched Britons Would Like to Know.
item.description:
As Britons swelter under yet another heat wave, forecasters are warning that a brutal summer is on course to become the hottest yet.

The Met Office, Britain’s weather agency, issued an amber warning — the second highest level — for Thursday in large parts of southeast England.

The extreme heat has remade summer for a country where many once escaped abroad to feel the blazing sun on their skins.

“An English summer is not the same anymore,” said Jacqui Browne, 67, as she sat on the brown grass of a London park.

On Thursday, temperatures in London are expected to reach 37 degrees Celsius (98.6 degrees Fahrenheit), according to a forecast by the Met Office.

There was a time when British summers were more temperate and marked by rain, but drought conditions have left large parts of the country parched.

The north, for example, is not as cool or green as usual, said Ms. Browne’s sister Janice Kennedy, 66, who was visiting from there.

“Even up north it’s quite warm,” Ms. Kennedy said. “Not like down here, but it’s quite warm up there, as well.”

Some, like Ms. Browne and Ms. Kennedy, still remember the summer of 1976, when repeated long spells of hot and dry weather made it the benchmark for hot summers. Now, that seems almost quaint.

The summer of 2022 stands out in memory for its intensity. It was then that Britain recorded a temperature above 40 degrees Celsius for the first time, according to the Met Office.

“Now it’s been overshadowed by the last three or four years,” Ms. Browne said.

By the end of this past July, Britain had already recorded 37 days of extreme heat, nearing a record set in 1995, when 39 days were recorded, according to figures from the weather agency.

Even if the last weeks of August are slightly cooler, the weather is still likely to break existing records, according to Met Office predictions.

“Another record-breaking summer now looks increasingly likely for the U.K., following the second-warmest June and second-warmest July on record, and yet another heat wave imminent,” Mike Kendon, the Met Office’s senior scientist, said in a statement this week.

“These statistics are a clear reminder — if one were needed — of the stark changes that we are seeing in the U.K.’s climate,” Mr. Kendon said.

Determining how a single heat event was influenced by climate change requires specific attribution studies. But scientists are certain that heat waves around the world are generally becoming more intense, more frequent and longer.

The heat has persuaded some to rethink how they spend their summers.

“I think you might find that is a real win for coastal towns,” Mike Jones, 55, said as he and friends cooled off in a London park. “I think there’ll be more staycations, too.”

His friend Caroline John noted a downside.

“When you go abroad, you have a cocktail and the sea,” she said. “Whereas, in London, you’re on the tube in the heat.”

The sweltering subway system is just one example of a region not built for heat, both agreed. Train lines have buckled in the heat, causing many delays over the summer.

“We’re not equipped, are we?” Ms. John, 50, said.

Britain’s weather agency warned that Thursday’s temperatures could affect heat-sensitive infrastructure in homes and businesses. And delays on the road and rail were expected, with potential health and welfare concerns for those stuck on the road.

The high temperatures could also lead to health complications for some, especially older people and those with vulnerabilities.

But for Anesta Logan, 61, who was in the park with Mr. Jones and Ms. John, the new British summer is an improvement over the cool ones she grew up with, to say nothing of the freezing winters.

“The hotter, the better,” she said. “People are always going to complain.”

]]>

item.title: Israel Evicted Settlers Besieging Palestinian Homes. Hours Later, They Were Back.
item.description:
The Israeli military evicted on Thursday about a dozen settlers who had besieged two Palestinian families in their West Bank homes, but several hours later settlers returned.

The Palestinian families had been trapped in their homes since Sunday by Israeli settlers, who had erected a tent nearby and, residents said, attacked them, including with rocks.

On Thursday morning, Israeli soldiers dismantled structures set up in the area by the settlers, confiscated some equipment, detained one settler and dispersed the rest, according to a military statement.

The operation came after heightened media attention, including the disclosure that one of the homes’ owners, Louai Abu Ridi, 46, is an American citizen. Mike Huckabee, the U.S. ambassador to Israel, condemned the settlers and said the United States had urged Israel to intervene.

“The actions of those doing this to this family’s home is criminal,” wrote Mr. Huckabee, a longtime supporter of the settler movement. He said, “Actions by those who carried out this horrific act of terror meant to intimidate and harass this family are disgusting.”

But just hours after the eviction operation ended in the village of Qusra, located in the northern West Bank, at least nine settlers returned to the site where they were previously encamped outside one of the homes, according to interviews with two residents and video footage reviewed by The New York Times.

“We are still under siege,” said Yousef Hassan, 30, who remains locked inside with his brother and his son. “If the army is here to take out the settlers, why are they not just doing it?” he asked.

Mr. Hassan said his family was running low on food and water.

The Israeli military did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

The military on Thursday also evicted settlers who had taken over another Palestinian house in nearby Jalud, according to its residents. Here, too, the settlers returned shortly after.

The military’s failure to keep settlers away from Qusra village after waiting several days before evicting them underscored the challenge it faces in contending with settler violence. It also highlights the deepening chaos across the West Bank, where hundreds of Israeli settlers have terrorized Palestinian communities with near-impunity all year.

Extremist settlers have carried out at least 1,380 attacks across 250 communities in 2026, according to U.N. data from late July. Those settlers have faced a near-total lack of consequences for their violence.

Former senior Israeli officials who previously oversaw the West Bank now warn that the military is losing its grip on the territory and allowing settlers to run wild.

“The Israeli military lost control in the West Bank,” said Guy Hazut, a reserve brigadier general who once oversaw parts of the territory as a commander.

The settlers seek to drive Palestinians from their land and have displaced several entire communities over the past three years.

The families in Qusra have refused to leave their homes even in the face of persistent attacks.

“We are very afraid,” said Aisha Hassan, 35, who said she was still besieged in her home with her elderly mother on Thursday. “But we won’t leave. Even if it’ll get us killed.”

Adam Rasgon and Gabby Sobelman contributed reporting.

]]>

item.title: Oil, Hunters and Dr. Phil: How a Longshot Project Is Shaking Up Greenland
item.description:
In one of the most remote towns on earth, on the frozen crust of Greenland’s east coast, the American oilman made his pitch.

Near to the very room where they were all sitting, he told a crowd of Greenlanders, could be as much as 13 billion barrels of oil. His company planned to drill two exploratory wells, and if it struck oil, it could be a major worldwide discovery bringing much-needed jobs, loads of tax money and relief to world energy markets.

The people who attended the meeting, which was held in June in an isolated town called Ittoqqortoormiit, had some questions.

Why would Greenland get only 15 percent of the profit?

What kind of chemicals would be used?

And what about the musk ox?

(Musk ox hunting is a big deal up there.)

The meeting wrapped up with a lot of unhappy people filing out, according to a video of it that was shared with The New York Times, and a showdown over oil exploration has now joined the cloud of issues swirling over Greenland.

The wildcat oil project is being pumped up by Dr. Phil McGraw, the TV personality known as Dr. Phil, and Gov. Jeff Landry of Louisiana, both powerful allies of President Trump. It’s the latest push by the MAGA camp to close in on this gigantic Arctic island that Mr. Trump threatened to annex and remains a fixation of his.

If the discovery is anything close to what the company says, and if it makes economic sense for major production — and those are two enormous ifs — this project could thrust Greenland into a radically different future, possibly as an Arctic petrostate.

But it’s off to a bumpy start. After a wave of negative publicity, protests by Greenlanders and a slip-up by the project’s organizers who have a drilling license, Greenland’s authorities tapped the brakes. This week the government pushed back the expected timeline for the permitting process to 2028.

The Texas-based firm leading the project, Greenland Energy Company, now says it will focus on drilling only one well, not two. And the delays are expected to cost millions. As a result, Greenland Energy’s share price has plummeted, trading at little more than a dollar, half its value from just days ago.

A few years ago, Greenland declared it was suspending oil exploration. The Arctic is among the fastest-warming regions in the world, and the Greenlandic government felt it was wrong to contribute more fossil fuel pollution.

But the oil prospectors in this case are operating with a valid license granted before the policy changed, according to documents reviewed by The New York Times. So Greenlandic officials, who have been trying to navigate the intense pressure Mr. Trump has put on them, find themselves in a tight spot.

They are more than aware that if they reflexively block Americans from drilling, especially at a time when world events have squeezed the global oil supply, that could give Mr. Trump the pretext he needs to return to his threats to “get” Greenland, “one way or the other.” At the same time, there’s obvious resistance from ordinary Greenlanders and government officials to the project.

“In a world where Donald Trump has pursued such a confrontational policy toward Greenland, you can’t help but be a little concerned,” said Mikkel Runge Olesen, a senior researcher at the Danish Institute for International Studies. “If you suddenly throw a major oil discovery into the mix, who knows what might happen.”

For months, the United States, Greenland and Denmark — the island’s former colonial master that still controls many of its affairs — have been locked in sticky negotiations over the island’s future. One key issue has been American access to Greenland’s natural resources.

Ever since Mr. Trump set his sights on the island, Greenland has become a magnet for investors and allies chasing Arctic resource dreams. But oil has never been easy.

Chevron and Shell prospected decades ago with no success. It’s incredibly expensive to build an oil industry from scratch in one of the most remote and inhospitable places on the planet. Most of Greenland is covered in ice. One major U.S. company, ARCO, decades ago sank today’s equivalent of $250 million — far more than the $80 million the current players have raised — into seismic studies in the same area, only to abandon the project in 1990.

“There are so many red flags here,” said Naaja Nathanielsen, Greenland’s former minister of natural resources and now a representative in Denmark’s Parliament. She says she hasn’t seen any hard data supporting the project’s tantalizing claims, adding, “I think they are selling hot air.”

Not so, say the backers of the project, a joint venture between Greenland Energy, the small, publicly traded U.S. company that raised the money, and 80 Mile Plc, a British outfit that acquired the drilling licenses several years ago.

Roderick McIllree, 80 Mile’s executive director and a board member of Greenland Energy, said this stretch of Greenland had the same geology as the North Sea oil fields, where European countries have extracted billions of barrels. And climate change is working in their favor, he said.

Warming temperatures mean less ice clogging Greenland’s coast, making any oil discovered cheaper to export than it would have been decades ago, he said.

One investor is the Citadel hedge fund, run by the investment titan Ken Griffin, and the Trump administration fully supports the project.

“Greenland could be exporting two million barrels of oil a day,” said Governor Landry, Mr. Trump’s special envoy to Greenland, in a Fox News interview in May. He added, “Think about what kind of pressure that would relieve in the Straits of Hormuz.”

Before the project is allowed to start, its plans, including a detailed environmental assessment, must be approved. But the organizers have been moving ahead anyway and recently carried out two disputed equipment transfers.

First, they brought in a barge of equipment from another part of Greenland on what authorities said was an expired permit. Jorgen Hammeken-Holm, the head of Greenland’s mineral resources department, called the move “naughty, naughty.”

Then, a few days later, they unloaded another piece of heavy equipment without proper notification, the authorities said.

“We have the police and the military,” Mr. Hammeken-Holm warned. “They can assist in dealing with unlawful activities if necessary.”

Mr. McIllree, the 80 Mile executive, admitted, “We kind of fell down.” He said the company apologized to Greenlandic officials.

The potentially oil-rich area, known as Jameson Land, is a highly protected environmental zone, an Arctic swampland of sorts, home to tenacious shrubs and musk ox, foxes and migrating birds like the pink-footed goose. The musk ox is prized for its meat and its fur, which is turned into a luxurious yarn.

All this has attracted Dr. Phil, who did a recent 44-minute podcast on the project. He titled the episode “Frozen Gold,” and according to documents on Greenland Energy’s website, the company has established “a wide-ranging partnership” with him to make a six-episode series on “this modern-day treasure hunt.”

His company did not respond to requests for comment about his involvement in the project. But on his podcast, Dr. Phil said he would soon head to the Arctic.

“I’m going to have to mug a kitten and get some mittens because I’m going to go up there and see this firsthand,” he said.

Ittoqqortoormiit (It-tok-kor-TOR-meet), population 329, is trying to make sense of all this. This spring, members of the local council seemed ready to negotiate and drafted a list of things they wanted from the oil company: a heated community pool, new hunting cabins and funding for residents to fly over Jameson Land in helicopters one last time before their hunting grounds were turned into an industrial site.

But the public meeting in June changed the mood.

Mr. McIllree conceded that the team that led the meeting didn’t show enough respect.

“They forgot whose house they were in,” he said.

Still, some residents support the project.

Aage Uugi Pike Barselajsen, a construction worker, said in a telephone interview that Ittoqqortoormiit desperately needed jobs.

“You have to think about the future and the money,” he explained. “Maybe Greenland could become like Dubai. That’s my dream.”

]]>

item.title: Female Afghans Erased From Public Life in Five Years of Taliban Rule
item.description:
The Taliban regained control of Afghanistan five years ago this week, returning to power after two decades and restoring an Islamic government that had severely restricted women’s rights.

In those few years, women and girls have been systematically erased from most public life, experts say. And, some add, the limitations imposed on half the population could hobble Afghanistan far into the future.

The harsh restrictions on women and girls are a return to conditions that prevailed the previous time the Taliban controlled Afghanistan, in the late 1990s. More than 160 decrees have been issued targeting women and girls, barring them from secondary and higher education and restricting their employment, movement, dress, speech and decision-making.

“No other country in modern times has dismantled the rights of half its population through law, policy and practice to the same extent,” the United Nations agency on women said on Wednesday. “At the same time, overlapping humanitarian and economic crises and deepening poverty are also having a disproportionate impact on women and girls.”

The official restrictions have reinforced social pressures, and many women say their communities increasingly press them to conform, a new U.N. Women report found, based on recent surveys. “Half a decade of escalating restrictions has narrowed where Afghan women can go, what they can do and how they can live,” it said. “The results are alarming.”

The agency surveyed about 5,000 Afghans in rural and urban communities this past spring and last year, asking women and men about life under the Taliban. There were some similarities in the genders’ answers — but some very stark differences as well.

Many Afghans surveyed expressed disappointment with the course of their lives in recent years. Still, women reported levels of isolation and distress that suggest a growing mental health crisis, the U.N. report said.

More than half of men surveyed — about 55 percent — said their lives were worse than they had expected they would be before August 2021, compared with 65 percent of women who reported a similar sentiment. But their reasoning was starkly different.

Male respondents reported frustration with a lack of economic opportunities, while many women also blamed reduced access to education, for themselves or their children, and rules restricting women’s jobs and lives.

“By closing off education and many forms of employment, these restrictions compound the economic pressures already felt by most women,” the U.N. report said, noting the “profound personal toll” the situation has had on women in Afghanistan. Many women reported rising stress, worry and pressure, “consistent with wider evidence of deteriorating mental health,” it added.

The report highlights the isolation many Afghan women now experience as a result of the restrictions. A vast majority of the women surveyed — 90 percent — said they must have a male family member’s permission to leave the house. And more than half said they went out only once or twice a month. Among male survey respondents, more than 95 percent reported leaving their homes daily.

Women and girls’ adherence to the new Taliban rules is increasingly reinforced by people around them, like relatives and neighbors. The U.N. report noted that nearly 40 percent of women surveyed this year said they felt more pressure than before to tailor their behavior for fear that those they know will report them for inappropriate dress, speech or actions.

“The Taliban have extended state control deep into the private sphere by transforming patriarchal norms into legal obligations and conscripting families into the enforcement of their ideology,” Belquis Ahmadi, a human rights lawyer and expert on Afghanistan, formerly at the United States Institute of Peace, wrote in a recent report on Taliban rule.

Human rights experts say that the crisis for women in Afghanistan has reached a critical point.

Afghanistan is the only country in the world to formally prohibit access to education for girls and women beyond the primary level. The longer women and girls are excluded from schools, institutions and public life, the more entrenched the restrictive system becomes, the further behind they fall and the fewer models there are, making their ability to recover ever less likely, jeopardizing the country’s long-term prospects.

“As a new generation of girls grows without an education, their future becomes increasingly dark,” UNESCO wrote in a statement this week, calling for the full restoration of the right to education for Afghan girls and women.

Ms. Ahmadi wrote in her analysis, “Behind every Taliban decree is a human story: a university student packing away her books, a teacher dismissed from the profession she loves, a judge forced into hiding, a doctor prevented from treating patients, an entrepreneur closing her business, or a young girl asking her parents why she is no longer allowed to learn while her brother walks freely to school.”

She argues that the international community must speak up for the silenced.

“The greatest danger facing Afghanistan today is not only that 20 million women and girls are being systematically erased from public life,” Ms. Ahmadi wrote. “It is that the world is slowly learning to live with it.”

]]>

item.title: Another Day of Extreme Heat Bakes Europe, but Relief Is on the Horizon
item.description:
Much of Europe was roasting on Friday in a dangerous, long-lasting heat wave — the fifth one on the continent this year — with the authorities in several countries warning of the serious risk of wildfires.

The scorching weather has strained infrastructure and severely disrupted everyday life and public services in several countries. More than 100 firefighters were deployed on Thursday to try and control a blaze that burned at least six properties in the West Midlands region of Britain, the local fire service said.

The heat, which has been linked to climate change, is driven by an area of high pressure that is colloquially known as a heat dome. This weather feature has been focused over the western part of the continent and is expected to shift east into Central Europe in the coming days, expanding into the Czech Republic, Germany and Poland.

Temperatures are forecast to slowly increase in Central Europe through the weekend and decrease to the west, as cooler Atlantic air and thunderstorms whip in from the west. It will still be hot in Spain and France, but the temperatures will not be quite as extreme as they have been.

High temperature warnings were in effect across Europe on Friday, with the most severe red-level warnings in portions of Italy and Switzerland.

Cooler weather was finally coming to some parts of Spain. AEMET, the country’s weather service, said that while the highest temperatures would broadly remain above 30 degrees Celsius (86 Fahrenheit) across much of the country on Friday and through the weekend, afternoon highs around 25 degrees Celsius (77 degrees Fahrenheit) were expected on the north coast. Forecasters warned of a chance of thunderstorms on Friday, particularly in the eastern, mountainous part of the country.

Scorching heat has spread across Italy since last week and will continue on Friday and through the weekend, with much of the country likely to see temperatures between 35 and 39 degrees Celsius (95 and 102 Fahrenheit), according to the Italian Air Force Meteorological Service. Rains could cool some areas, at least temporarily, on Sunday.

Britain has been baking for days. The Met Office, the country’s weather service, said the country was on track to record its warmest summer on record for average temperature, breaking a record set just last year. Friday was forecast to be slightly cooler than recent days were, with the hottest temperatures reaching 34 degrees Celsius (93 Fahrenheit). A cold front was expected to pull fresh air into the country on Saturday, creating less humid conditions, forecasters said. There’s a possibility of some rain after the weekend and into next week.

Météo-France, France’s weather service, reported that the peak of the heat wave was Thursday, but much of the country was expected to see afternoon highs yet again between 35 and 40 degrees Celsius (95 and 104 Fahrenheit) on Friday. Temperatures are gradually predicted to fall, beginning along the English Channel and Atlantic Coast on Friday and spreading across the rest of the country through the weekend.

Germany’s weather service, the Deutscher Wetterdienst, predicted that the highest temperatures on Friday and Saturday could reach up to 38 degrees Celsius (100 Fahrenheit), particularly in the west and the southwest. Sunday was likely to be cooler, with rain in the forecast and the highest temperatures probably settling at 32 degrees Celsius (90 Fahrenheit).

The heat has intensified the ongoing severe threat of wildfires across Europe. Fires have burned more than 1.4 million acres across the European Union so far this year. It’s smaller than the area that burned by this time last year, the worst year on record, but double the 20 year average of scorched land.

The European Forest Fire Information System said that a large area of Central Europe, stretching from Germany through Poland and into the Balkans, as well as parts of Britain, Ireland, France and Sweden, would remain under “very extreme” fire conditions at least through next week.

Staying cool and hydrating often are the two most important things to do to avoid feeling sick and discomfort in extreme heat. Here are some other ways to keep cool:

Block out the windows in your home — especially those that get afternoon sun — with a blanket or a darker sheet during the day to keep the heat out. At night, keep windows open and run fans to circulate the air.

Spritz your skin with a mist of cool or room-temperature water or wipe your forehead with a cool cloth. Cold showers can also help you cool down.

If you need to be outdoors, put ice cubes in your water bottle and drink cool liquids. If you plan to exercise, douse your head in cold water. Swimming is also a great way to exercise and keep cool.

When exploring or sightseeing, seek out cooler attractions such as museums, cathedrals or even subterranean exhibitions. Some cities have created public spaces to cool down: Barcelona has climate shelters and Paris has drinking fountains, for example. London has a Cool Spaces map to find spots.

Watch out for signs of heat stroke. The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention lists some of them as dizziness, a rapid pulse, nausea, headache and fainting. But symptoms can vary.

item.title: Farage Wins Special U.K. Election That He Initiated, as Expected
item.description:
Nigel Farage, the leader of Reform U.K., Britain’s populist right-wing party, won a special election on Thursday that he initiated when he resigned amid a parliamentary investigation into possible financial impropriety.

As expected, Mr. Farage easily defeated dozens of fringe and novelty candidates, including Count Binface, who wears a trash-can-themed costume. None of Britain’s other major parties participated in the race, the results of which were announced early Friday. They called it a political stunt engineered by the Reform leader to distract from the investigation.

Mr. Farage received 22,239 votes, or 63 percent. Count Binface, a character played by Jon Harvey, 46, a writer and comedian, received 9,455 votes, or 27 percent. Mr. Binface’s previous best result was 1 percent in a London mayoral election.

Turnout was slightly higher than expected, with 35,401 voters — 44 percent of those eligible — participating in the election.

In a departure from political tradition in Britain, Mr. Farage did not attend the official announcement of the result. At a Reform U.K. event called “Farage Fest” a few hours earlier, he pre-emptively announced that he had won. And he told supporters: “I am damned if I am going to stand on a stage, having won a resounding victory, a ringing endorsement of all that I’ve tried to fight for and you’ve tried to fight for, and be demeaned and humiliated by nobodies.”

The Reform leader is under investigation by the parliamentary standards commissioner for failing to declare a 5 million pound gift, about $6.7 million, that he received in the weeks before the 2024 general election. Mr. Farage has given varying explanations for the gift, which he received from Christopher Harborne, a British crypto-billionaire based in Thailand. At one point Mr. Farage said it was a reward for Brexit, while at other times he has said it was to pay for his personal security.

Last month, Mr. Farage abruptly resigned the seat, which he had held since 2024, and immediately announced he would run again in the ensuing by-election, saying he wanted a new mandate from his constituents in Clacton, a coastal area in Essex, England, to show that his voters did not care about the allegations.

“The people of Clacton should be the judges of my actions,” he said in his resignation speech in July. “This will be a people-versus-the-establishment by-election.”

Mr. Farage referred in the speech to the standards investigation into the Harborne gift, and also said that “yet another standards investigation is underway.” Days before, The Sunday Times of London had reported that one of Mr. Farage’s close aides, George Cottrell, had provided undisclosed benefits to Mr. Farage, including security, social media employees and accommodation. Mr. Farage has since said he did not need to report the benefits because they were received before his election to Parliament.

The parliamentary code of conduct says that lawmakers must register any benefits received in the 12 months before they are elected, unless they could be considered “purely personal gifts.” It adds: “Both the possible motive of the giver and the use to which the gift is to be put should be considered. If there is any doubt, the benefit should be registered.”

Mr. Farage is an ally of President Trump who has long warned of an “invasion” of migrants and railed against “the establishment.” In May, Reform won almost 1,500 seats on municipal councils. But its overall share of the vote was only about 26 percent, down from more than 30 percent the previous year.

Several recent polls have shown support for the party falling to under 25 percent and Labour taking the lead. The polls have shown a continued decline as the accusations about improper disclosure of financial support have increased.

Reform officials were always very confident, however, that Mr. Farage would recapture his seat in Clacton, which voted by a large margin for Brexit, his signature cause. The last time he ran there, during the 2024 general election, he won with 46.2 percent of the vote, and the Conservative Party candidate came second with 27.9 percent.
